newsitem.title: UK: British scientists urge renewed space effort.
newsitem.headline: British scientists urge renewed space effort.

text.p: Two space disasters in six months have badly knocked efforts to explore our solar system, but British space scientists on Tuesday urged governments to get back in the game as soon as possible.
They said it would take a relatively small investment to re-create the Cluster experiment that crashed back to Earth with the French Ariane 5 rocket last June.
Last weekend's failure of a Russian Mars probe gave added importance to a renewal of the European effort.
"Right now, a cost-efficient way to rebuild almost all that was lost is on offer," the scientists, an informal grouping of several who worked on the project, said in a statement.
They said the European Space Agency (ESA) would meet next week to decide whether to go ahead with the effort, dubbed Phoenix after the mythical bird that rises from its own ashes.
The re-born project would cost only 195 million pounds ($325 million), compared to the original 430 million pound ($720 million) mission cost.
"We've got to get across our view that this is a bargain," said David Southwood of London's Imperial College, who chaired the ESA's science committee until this summer.
Britain's contribution would be seven million pounds, spent mostly in building delicate measuring instruments.
"You could not imagine getting that much science for that little money," said Steve Schwartz, a space scientist at Queen Mary and Westfield College.
Ariane 5, a test launcher for French company Arianespace, was exploded by its operators just 40 seconds after liftoff because of a software failure that made in unsteerable.
It took with it the Cluster experiment, a set of four spacecraft that would orbit the Earth, studying how solar flares and solar wind affected the Earth's magnetic field.

The idea was to eventually be able to predict magnetic storms just as weather is predicted now. This is important because such storms affect satellites and communications, including mobile phones, and can cause widespread power outages.
The ESA has a proposal to re-build Cluster using spare parts, but each of the 20 countries involved must stump up its original contribution as well.
"What we can do is get back most of the science and most of the money that has already been spent," Southwood told a news conference.

Andrew Fazakerley of University College London's Mullard Space Science Laboratory said the ESA had to move now, while the teams that assembled Cluster were still there. Soon the skilled scientists and engineers would have to move onto other projects.
"If we wait, we will have to start again from scratch," Fazakerley said.
They could re-create the instruments cheaply because most of the cost involved research, design and testing.

Southwood said the weekend Mars-96 disaster, when Russia's Mars exploration launcher failed in orbit and tumbled back to Earth, showed that "making friends" with countries that had a space programme was not enough.
"A hiccup in the Russian programme makes it even more important that western Europe secures its space effort," he said.
